AI.tldr: TabooRAG is a black-box, transferable blocking attack on retrieval-augmented generation systems that exploits the homogeneity of safety alignment in modern LLMs. By crafting query-specific adversarial documents on a surrogate model, it achieves high cross-model blocking rates—up to 96%—revealing critical vulnerabilities in standardized safety mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Despite the growing use of safety-aligned LLMs in RAG systems, their susceptibility to blocking attacks persists. Traditional methods like adversarial suffixes are less effective against modern defenses. The authors are motivated by the observation that safety mechanisms themselves can be exploited due to LLMs' heightened sensitivity to risk signals, and that alignment practices are increasingly homogeneous, enabling cross-model attack transfer.
AI.method: The authors propose TabooRAG, a black-box transferable blocking attack framework that exploits alignment homogeneity—overlapping safety criteria across LLMs. It generates adversarial documents by optimizing against a surrogate LLM and transfers them to target RAG systems without model access. A query-aware strategy library is introduced to enhance optimization efficiency by reusing successful prior strategies.
AI.result: TabooRAG achieves up to 96% blocking success rate on GPT-5.2 and demonstrates strong transferability across 7 modern LLMs and 3 datasets under strict black-box conditions. It outperforms prior methods, showing stable performance even without access to the target model or its alignment logic.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that the standardization of safety alignment across modern LLMs introduces a shared, exploitable vulnerability in RAG systems, exemplified by the high transferability and effectiveness of the proposed TabooRAG attack, underscoring the need for more robust defensive measures.

title: OMNIINTENT: A Trusted Intent-Centric Framework for User-Friendly Web3
summary:
The increasingly complex Web3 ecosystem and decentralized finance (DeFi) landscape demand ever higher levels of technical expertise and financial literacy from participants. The Intent-Centric paradigm in DeFi has thus emerged in response, which allows users to focus on their trading intents rather than the underlying execution details. However, existing approaches, including Typed-intent design and LLM-driven solver, trade off expressiveness, trust, privacy, and composability.
  We present OMNIINTENT, a language-runtime co-design that reconciles these requirements. OMNIINTENT introduces ICL, a domain-specific Intent-Centric Language for precise yet flexible specification of triggers, actions, and runtime constraints; a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE)-based compiler that compiles intents into signed, state-bound transactions inside an enclave; and an execution optimizer that constructs transaction dependency graphs for safe parallel batch submission and a mempool-aware feasibility checker that predicts execution outcomes. Our full-stack prototype processes diverse DeFi scenarios, achieving 89.6% intent coverage, up to 7.3x throughput speedup via parallel execution, and feasibility-prediction accuracy up to 99.2% with low latency.

AI.tldr: OMNIINTENT is a language-runtime co-design for Intent-Centric DeFi that introduces a domain-specific language (ICL), a TEE-based secure compiler, and an execution optimizer, achieving high intent coverage, throughput, and accurate feasibility prediction.
AI.motivation: Existing Intent-Centric DeFi systems face trade-offs between expressiveness, trust, privacy, and composability, limiting usability and security for users lacking technical expertise.
AI.method: OMNIINTENT proposes: (1) ICL, a domain-specific language for specifying intents with triggers, actions, and constraints; (2) a TEE-based compiler that securely compiles intents into signed, state-bound transactions; and (3) an execution optimizer with transaction dependency graph construction for parallel batch execution and a mempool-aware feasibility checker for outcome prediction.
AI.result: The prototype achieves 89.6% intent coverage across diverse DeFi scenarios, up to 7.3x throughput improvement via parallel execution, and up to 99.2% accuracy in feasibility prediction with low latency.
AI.conclusion: OMNIINTENT effectively reconciles expressiveness, security, privacy, and composability in Intent-Centric DeFi through language-runtime co-design and TEE-based execution, enabling scalable and trustworthy automated DeFi interactions.

title: CAM-LDS: Cyber Attack Manifestations for Automatic Interpretation of System Logs and Security Alerts
summary: Log data are essential for intrusion detection and forensic investigations. However, manual log analysis is tedious due to high data volumes, heterogeneous event formats, and unstructured messages. Even though many automated methods for log analysis exist, they usually still rely on domain-specific configurations such as expert-defined detection rules, handcrafted log parsers, or manual feature-engineering. Crucially, the level of automation of conventional methods is limited due to their inability to semantically understand logs and explain their underlying causes. In contrast, Large Language Models enable domain- and format-agnostic interpretation of system logs and security alerts. Unfortunately, research on this topic remains challenging, because publicly available and labeled data sets covering a broad range of attack techniques are scarce. To address this gap, we introduce the Cyber Attack Manifestation Log Data Set (CAM-LDS), comprising seven attack scenarios that cover 81 distinct techniques across 13 tactics and collected from 18 distinct sources within a fully open-source and reproducible test environment. We extract log events that directly result from attack executions to facilitate analysis of manifestations concerning command observability, event frequencies, performance metrics, and intrusion detection alerts. We further present an illustrative case study utilizing an LLM to process the CAM-LDS. The results indicate that correct attack techniques are predicted perfectly for approximately one third of attack steps and adequately for another third, highlighting the potential of LLM-based log interpretation and utility of our data set.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CAM-LDS, a publicly available, labeled log dataset covering diverse cyber attack techniques, and demonstrates its utility in enabling LLM-based, domain-agnostic log analysis for intrusion detection.
AI.motivation: Existing automated log analysis methods rely heavily on manual configurations and lack semantic understanding; moreover, there is a scarcity of comprehensive, labeled log datasets to support research on cyber attack manifestations.
AI.method: The authors developed CAM-LDS—a reproducible, open-source dataset with logs from 18 sources across 7 attack scenarios, covering 81 techniques and 13 tactics. They extract logs directly tied to attack steps and conduct a case study using LLMs to interpret these logs and infer attack techniques.
AI.result: The LLM-based case study shows that attack techniques are correctly predicted for about one-third of steps and adequately for another third, demonstrating the dataset's usefulness and the potential of LLMs in log analysis.
AI.conclusion: CAM-LDS fills a critical gap in cyber security research by providing a rich, labeled dataset, and shows that LLMs can effectively interpret system logs semantically, paving the way for more automated and explainable intrusion detection.

title: Statistical Effort Modelling of Game Resource Localisation Attacks
summary:
Evidence on the effectiveness of Man-At-The-End (MATE) software protections, such as code obfuscation, has mainly come from limited empirical research. Recently, however, an automatable method was proposed to obtain statistical models of the required effort to attack (protected) software. The proposed method was sketched for a number of attack strategies but not instantiated, evaluated, or validated for those that require human interaction with the attacked software.
  In this paper, we present a full instantiation of the method to obtain statistical effort models for game resource localisation attacks, which represent a major step towards creating game cheats, a prime example of MATE attacks. We discuss in detail all relevant aspects of our instantiation and the results obtained for two game use cases. Our results confirm the feasibility of the proposed method and its utility for decision support for users of software protection tools. These results open up a new avenue for obtaining models of the impact of software protections on reverse engineering attacks, which will scale much better than empirical research involving human participants.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a fully instantiated, automatable method to model the effort required for human-involving reverse engineering attacks (specifically game resource localization), demonstrating its feasibility and value for evaluating software protection mechanisms.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of scalable and systematic empirical methods to evaluate the effectiveness of MATE software protections like code obfuscation, especially for attacks involving human interaction. Existing research is limited, necessitating an automatable, statistically grounded approach to model attack effort.
AI.method: The authors fully instantiated a previously proposed automatable method to create statistical models estimating the effort required for game resource localization attacks, which involve human-in-the-loop strategies. They applied and evaluated the method in two real game use cases, detailing all components including attack scenarios, measurement of effort, and model derivation.
AI.result: The instantiation successfully produced statistical effort models for game resource localization attacks in two use cases. The method demonstrated scalability and practical utility in evaluating software protection efficacy without relying on human-intensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: The study confirms the feasibility and utility of the proposed method for generating statistical effort models for reverse engineering attacks, particularly in the context of game resource localization, enabling better decision-making for software protection strategies.
